newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Left urges changes in 97/98 budget.
newsitem.headline: India's Left urges changes in 97/98 budget.

text.p: India's four leading left-wing parties on Monday urged Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's government to modify the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, due to be taken up by parliament this week.
The Left Front issued a statement after a meeting calling for changes in the areas of insurance, taxes, divestment in state enterprises, public distribution, customs duties and excise duties.

"The Left parties are of the considered opinion that certain changes are required in the budget proposals and Finance Bill which will be in keeping with the interests of the people and the country," the Left Front said.
The Left Front is comprised of the two main communist parties, the Revolutionary Socialist Party and the Forward Bloc, all components of Gujral's United Front coalition.
The parties said it was opposed to opening up the health insurance sector to private firms.

"In the interests of strengthening the public sector, the proposal for disinvestment of the PSU (public sector unit) shares in the profitable units and in core and strategic areas should not be proceeded with," it said.
The parties urged the government to increase spending on the public distribution system to protect the interests of the poor.

"In the taxation proposals, there are big concessions given to the corporate sector and the richer strata," it said. "The lowering of corporate taxes and other similar concessions to the affluent sections should be modified."
Earlier on Monday, Sitaram Yechury, politburo member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), said the Left Front wanted to amend the tax proposals relating to the two higher income groups.
In his budget presented on February 28, former finance minister P. Chidambaram had proposed reducing the tax rate on annual income from 40,000 to 60,000 rupees to 10 percent from 15 percent.
The tax rate on income from 60,000 to 150,000 rupees would be cut to 20 percent from 30 percent, while the rate on incomes above 150,000 rupees would be reduced to 30 percent from 40.
The Left Front said the lowering of import duties on items which affect the domestic industry and encourage large-scale imports of luxury goods should be reconsidered.
"In the excise duties, the way the reclassification of small-scale units and the excise duties have been imposed, they will have adverse affect on the small-scale sector," the statement said.
"The Left parties decided to discuss their suggestions with the prime minister and the United Front government so that suitable changes can be made," it said.
Parliament reconvenes on Wednesday to take up the tax and spending proposals for 1997/98.
